title: Pipkin's Button Adventure
markdown:
It was a bright sunshiny morning, the kind that made Pipkin the piglet’s floppy pink ears wiggle. He was playing with Marlo the magpie, whose feathers sparkled like dewdrops on a web.

They had a little wooden box of buttons: red as happy ladybugs, blue as sky, tiny green that twinkled like emeralds. Pipkin lined them by colour and size. Marlo watched them catch the sun.

Pipkin, curious, gave the box a tiny nudge with his snout. Whoosh. The box tipped. Buttons tumbled like coloured candies. Red ones rolled under the picnic blanket. Blue ones headed for the garden gate. Green ones winked behind a cushion.

“Oh dear.” Ears drooped. A mess, and a worry to match.

Marlo swooped from a branch, good at spotting treasure. “We can find them all. A treasure hunt.”

“There are so many.” Pipkin’s snout twitched. A big job for a small piglet.

“A hunt is better with a friend.” Marlo puffed his chest. “The bakery first.”

The bakery was warm and smelled of bread and cinnamon rolls that had just decided to be themselves. Pipkin’s tummy rumbled a greeting. They tiptoed past the round ovens; the air hugged. A tray of buns steamed like little clouds. Pipkin sniffed the flour sacks, got a dusty nose, and sneezed a tiny achoo that made a puff like winter. Marlo fluttered high, sharp eyes on shelves of treats, then low along the skirting where crumbs kept secrets.

“A sparkly red one. Behind the big gingerbread cookie. The one with the currant smile.”

Pipkin trotted, ears wobbling, nudged it free without toppling the cookie, which would have been a different adventure. “Hooray.”

They found a blue button in a bag of sugar. Pipkin gave it a lick. Sweet, and a little gritty. They looked under wooden chairs, behind mixing bowls, and in the shadow of a rolling pin that had seen things. Seven buttons in the bakery, lined for a moment on a cool tile so Marlo could count twice. A very good start. The baker, who was a kind loaf of a person, pretended not to see the flour on Pipkin’s ears and offered a crumb that was not a button.

“Where next?” Pipkin felt happier already.

“Cozy places hide things,” said Marlo, circling once.

“The barn.” Ears perked. Soft hay stacked like sleepy hills. Sleepy cows mooing a soft song, one of them dreaming of clover. Gold sun-stripes on the dusty floor, motes dancing as if they too were buttons. Hay tickled Pipkin’s tummy. They searched straw piles, sneezed more politely this time, and asked a hen if she had seen sparkle. The hen had seen breakfast. Marlo sat on a high beam, eyes like little stars.

“Found one.” He swooped a shiny green button from beside a sleeping kitten. The kitten blinked, yawned, and returned to the important work of nap. Pipkin found a deep purple button under a loose floorboard, smooth and cool. Three more in the barn. Each find made the next one likelier.

“We’re doing well,” said Pipkin, with a wiggle.

“Wild places hide the trickiest,” said Marlo, tail twitching.

“The blackberry hedge.” Eyes sparkled. Edge of the farm, juicy dark berries shimmering. They pushed gently through prickles, careful of snout and wings. Marlo flew above and called the way.

“Down here. Near the biggest juiciest berry.”

Pipkin waddled. Next to a plump dark berry sat a gold button, brighter than the others, a tiny piece of sun. A little farther, tangled in a green vine: shiny silver and pearly white, the last two.

“We found all the buttons.” Pipkin danced on the grass, a small piglet parade.

They gathered the treasure in a pile. “What shall we do with them?” Pipkin asked, eyes shining.

Marlo tilted his head. “We can make something to remember the hunt. Something made by us.”

They spent the rest of the afternoon sewing the buttons onto a big soft cushion. Pipkin pushed thread with his snout. Marlo tied knots with his beak. When they sat on it, bakery-warm, barn-dusty, hedge-sweet, the cushion winked like the morning box, only this time nothing rolled away unless they chose to play again.
